passages.text: Have you ever wondered why the sky is blue during day-time, and not yellow or any other colour? Some people think the sky is blue because of the water in the Earth’s atmosphere. But the sky is blue in the desert which is an extremely dry place. Others think the sky is blue because of sunlight that is reflected off the ocean and back to the sky. But the sky is blue in areas that are far from the sea, like Johannesburg, so that doesn’t make sense.

As I discussed previously, the sky is blue because tiny particles in the atmosphere (dust, clumps of air molecules, microscopic water droplets) are better at deflecting shorter wavelength blue light than they are at deflecting longer wavelength red light. As sunlight passes through the atmosphere, enough blue light is deflected (or more technically Rayleigh scattered) by these particles to give the atmosphere an overall blue glow. The sun itself is slightly reddened by this process because a fraction of its blue light is deflected away before it reaches our eyes.

One sunny day between battles, they sat under a beautiful blue sky, curious about its color. Younger readers might enjoy knowing that our sky appears blue because molecules in the air scatter sunlight in every direction. Blue light has shorter waves and gets scattered more easily than red or yellow light. That's why we see a bright blue sky!

For instance, consider day and night. Daytime brings bright sunlight and increased activity levels, while night offers calmness and relaxation under the moonlight. Both serve essential functions, contributing to our daily rhythms and overall wellbeing. Without either, chaos could ensue.
Earth rotates on its axis, causing day-night cycles. Humans organize their daily routines accordingly. Adjust your sleep-wake cycle to match the local time zone where you reside.
- The sun and moon had previously been created at some point. It is now that the first eye evolves which could distinguish between day and night.
We have got the answer! The seasons occur on earth is because of the tilt of the axis of rotation of Earth (or Inclination of axis of rotation).

A season is a period of the year marked by specific weather conditions and day lengths. There are four distinct seasons – Spring, Summer, Autumn (or Fall), and Winter. These occur due to the tilt of Earth's axis as it revolves around the Sun. When one hemisphere of the earth tilts towards the Sun, it receives stronger sunlight causing warmer temperatures; hence, we have summer. Conversely, when the opposite hemisphere tilts away, it gets less direct sunlight resulting in colder temperatures – thus, giving us winter.

Seasons are differences in the Earth’s orbit around the Sun. The Earth is slightly tilted. that is what causes the seasons! Places around the Earth experience the same seasons, but they might not all feel the same.

Next, they mentioned the Moon, which changes shape every few days. Sometimes it's round like a ball (full moon), sometimes it's half-moon shaped, and other times it's just a thin line (new moon). The last quarter moon was coming on December 5th. Little Timmy wondered, "Why does the Moon change shape?" Shane happily answered, "That happens because the Moon orbits around Earth, and as it moves, we only see parts of it lit up by the Sun."

The sky changes it’s appearance each month as the moon waxes and wanes. Some nights when the moon is full it’s like someone turned on a bright spotlight. Other nights when a new moon is approaching it is near impossible to make out the shape of your hand right in front of your face.

In this blog post we will take a closer look at the eight different stages and what they actually mean. The reason we see a different moon shape is that light comes from the sun and depending on the position of the moon we see changes in its illumination.

Sunlight is a portion of the electromagnetic radiation given off by the Sun, in particular infrared, visible, and ultraviolet light. On Earth, sunlight is filtered through the Earth's atmosphere and is obvious as daylight when the Sun is above the horizon. When the direct solar radiation is not blocked by clouds, it is experienced as sunshine, a combination of bright light and radiant heat. When it is blocked by clouds or reflects off other objects, it is experienced as diffused light.

The sun is a star, a hot ball of glowing gases at the heart of our solar system. Its influence extends far beyond the orbits of distant Neptune and Pluto. Without the sun’s intense energy and heat, there would be no life on Earth. And though it is special to us, there are billions of stars like our sun scattered across the Milky Way galaxy.
The ‘sun‘ is a star in our solar system around which the earth and other planets orbit. ‘Son‘ is a male offspring. If you have children, the male child is your son.

Bolt replied, “Stars appear to twinkle because of Earth's atmosphere. Light bends and refracts around particles, creating different colors and brightness. It's like comparing starlight to our scale of 1 to 10!"

One day, while observing the night sky, Bai Lianhua asked, "Why do stars twinkle?" Curious, Long Autian searched for answers and learned about something called 'light pollution.' When city lights mix with star light, it causes the stars to appear dimmer or brighter unpredictably – making them twinkle!

Stars appear to twinkle “because their light travels through the atmosphere, which has wind and pressure variations that deflect the light on small scales,” Hébert says. These atmospheric perturbations also can alter galaxies’ appearances.

According to the general theory of relativity, a black hole is a region of space from which nothing, including light, can escape. It is the result of the deformation of spacetime caused by a very compact mass. Around a black hole there is an undetectable surface which marks the point of no return, called an event horizon. It is called "black" because it absorbs all the light that hits it, reflecting nothing, just like a perfect black body in thermodynamics.

A black hole is a region in space where gravitational forces are so great that not even light can escape. Gas and dust funnel towards a black hole in an accretion disk, swirling around and into the void like water down a drain. This process of accretion generates copious amounts of light -- predominantly X-ray radiation, particularly in the innermost (hottest) regions of the accretion disk.

Black holes are regions of space where matter is squeezed together so densely that everything, including light, becomes trapped in its gravitational pull. As a result, it is impossible to see the "hole" itself, since no light can escape it. But theoretically, scientists should be able to use an EHT to see a black hole's event horizon – the gravitational point of no return for anything being sucked inside.

- Goes around in circles: Our planet travels around the Sun at a speed of 67,000 miles per hour (107,827 kilometers per hour). That’s quite a journey every year. Even at that speed, Earth takes 365 days (and six hours) to complete a single trip.

The sun is 150 kilometers (93 million miles) away from the Earth. If you drove there at 96.6 kilometers per hour (60 miles per hour), it would take 177 years to reach it. Still, sometimes large eruptions from the sun reach man-made satellites and disrupt communications devices. It takes light eight minutes to get from the sun to Earth.

Earth takes about 365.24 days to complete one full trip around the Sun. As our planet moves along its path, different parts receive varying amounts of sunlight based on their location relative to the Sun. This difference results in seasonal variations we experience as spring, summer, autumn (or fall), and winter.

Mars is named after the Romans God of War. It’s also called the Red Planet because the iron oxide on its surface makes it appear red.

Mars is often called the Red Planet because it appears reddish when we look at it through telescopes. But why does it look like that? Well, just like here on Earth, there are rocks and dust covering Mars' surface. However, unlike Earth, iron oxide (or rust!) gives them their distinctive color. Imagine if all the dirt in your backyard turned red; that would be quite a sight!

Mars is often called the Red Planet because of its reddish appearance in the night sky. When we look at pictures of Mars taken by spacecraft, we can see that its surface is covered with rust-colored dust. Iron oxide - also known as iron rust - gives this dust its distinctive color. You might think of it as if the entire planet had a bad case of sunburn!
The Earth's tides are caused by the gravitational pull of primarily the moon, but also the sun on the Earth's oceans, as well as the Earth's own rotation.

Tides: When we think about the ocean, many of us imagine crashing waves along sandy shores. Those surges are partly caused by something called 'tides'. Tides result from the gravitational pull exerted by the moon and sun on Earth. As they rise and fall, they create two high tides and two low tides each day where you might notice seawater covering parts of the shoreline then receding back out again.

If you have ever been to the ocean, you were probably fascinated by the phenomena of the waves crashing against the shorelines as the tides came in. The ocean’s tides are the product of gravitational pull of the sun and the moon, as well as, the Earth’s rotation. It causes the ocean waters to be raised and lowered from time to time. The tides have cycles of twelve and one half hours, twice per day, and are easily predictable.

As the space station orbits, it is in a state of free fall, meaning only gravity is pulling on it. If the station is falling around Earth, then so is everything inside the station. The free falling is what produces microgravity. Since everything inside the station is falling, dropped objects tend to float. If astronauts do not want an object to float, they must secure it to the walls, floor or ceiling. Sometimes, they stick food packages to the wall with Velcro®.

Up on the International Space Station, gravity certainly does exist, but objects in orbit are in continuous free fall, effectively falling sideways in a gradual loop around the planet. This renders them weightless; zero gravity means there’s essentially zero acceleration towards the earth. That being said, the ISS does keep falling ‘downwards’, so to speak, due to a phenomenon known as orbital decay. They periodically perform small ‘re-boosts’ about once a month to increase their altitude above the Earth.

A space station is like a big apartment building orbiting Earth where astronauts live and work. They conduct experiments, observe our planet, and prepare for missions beyond our atmosphere. These 'apartments' have rooms for eating, sleeping, working, and even playing games! Since there's no natural gravity in space, astronauts use centrifugal force to create artificial gravity by spinning the space station. Imagine going round and round on a playground merry-go-round – that pulling feeling you get when trying to walk away is similar to artificial gravity!

What we may call "falling stars" or "shooting stars" are not really stars at all, but meteors, chunks of rock or ice that enter the earth's atmosphere from outer space. Friction with the air causes the meteors to burn, creating that glow you see in the sky.

Among the most spectacular sights of the night sky are shooting stars. Unlike most celestial objects, shooting stars exist only briefly as they blaze across the sky and then suddenly fade. Shooting stars appear every night, as do several meteor showers in which dozens of shooting stars can appear every hour. For these reasons, many myths about shooting stars exist.

With its gently cantering rhythm and alliteration, ‘Star Light, Star Bright’, commemorates and propagates the ancient tradition of wishing to the stars. The tradition takes many forms, variously invoking the power of the first star; nine stars; a shooting star. The most enduring myth is that shooting stars are caused by the Roman gods peering over the clouds into the mortal realm, and they will hear you (and perhaps heed you) when you speak your wish aloud.

According to Wiktionary, a volcano is "a mountain that contains a magma chamber attached to the mantle of the planet or moon and which periodically erupts forth, usually explosively, with lava and volcanic gases." There are many volcanoes, both active or dormant and extinct.

A volcano is an opening, or rupture, in a planet's surface or crust, which allows hot, molten rock, ash, and gases to escape from below the surface. Volcanic activity involving the extrusion of rock tends to form mountains or features like mountains over a period of time.

A volcano is essentially an opening in the Earth's crust through which magma (molten rock), gas, and ash escape during an eruption. To better comprehend how volcanoes function, let us first familiarize ourselves with the various components that constitute their structure:

Earthquakes are caused by the movement of the tectonic plates that make up the surface of the Earth. These plates are in constant slow motion as they respond to rock that’s flowing deep within the Earth. Earthquakes generally happen at faults – areas where the edges of these plates rub together. As the plates stick and push against each other, tension builds up. Eventually, when the rock at the edges of the plates can’t withstand any more strain, the rock breaks. The shaking that results is the earthquake.

Before diving into the technology behind seismic design, let us take a step back and examine what causes earthquakes and why they pose significant challenges to built environments. Earthquakes are primarily caused by tectonic plate movements along fault lines, resulting in sudden energy release that propagates through the ground as waves. These seismic waves exert forces on structures, leading to potential deformation, displacement, and even collapse.

Before we delve into the specifics of earthquake-resistant design, it's important to understand what causes earthquakes and how they behave. At their core, earthquakes are caused by sudden movements along fault lines in the earth's crust. These movements release energy in waves that radiate outward from the epicenter of the quake. Depending on the magnitude of the earthquake and the properties of the surrounding geological formations, these waves can cause significant damage to buildings and infrastructure.

Sunlight is made up of different colors, and when it passes through these drops, it bends and spreads out, creating a stunning arc of color we call a rainbow!"

When the sunlight strikes raindrops in the air, they act like a prism and form a rainbow. The rainbow is a division of white light into many beautiful colors. These take the shape of a long round arch, with its path high above, and its two ends apparently beyond the horizon. There is, according to legend, a boiling pot of gold at one end. People look, but no one ever finds it.

Because of this, the top of the rainbow appears red and the bottom violet. Such a rainbow is known as a primary rainbow. It is formed by light which has only bee reflected once inside the water droplets. Individual colors of the spectrum reaching one observer com from different raindrops.

The sound of thunder is caused by a shock wave created in the air, similar to the sonic boom of a supersonic jet plane. The lightning occurs first and the thunder occurs a fraction of a second later.

Now let's think about rainfall – something very important for all life forms on Earth. Rain happens when warm, moist air rises, cools down, and condenses forming clouds, eventually leading to precipitation. But where does this moisture come from? Often it comes from large bodies of water such as oceans, seas, and lakes. When the warm, wet air moves over land, it brings much-needed rainfall. However, factors such as mountains, valleys, and even urbanization can influence localized rainfall patterns.

Rain is one type of precipitation - water that falls from the sky to the Earth's surface. It begins as tiny water droplets high up in the atmosphere when warm air rises and cools down. This cooling causes the water vapor in the air to condense, forming clouds. When enough water collects together, gravity pulls it downwards, creating raindrops!

Rain is droplets of water that are condensed as a result of evaporation. During the water cycle formation of clouds takes place. Rain is also called precipitation. Water is absorbed from different water bodies, a large amount of which vaporizes and enters the atmospheric air.

One day, while answering questions on Quora about meteorology, I stumbled across this one: “What are clouds on Earth made of?” Among the choices were rain, ozone, carbon dioxide gas, and water vapor. It struck me as odd because although these elements are all part of our atmosphere, they aren't what actually constitutes clouds. So, I took it upon myself to explain, using terms a fifth grader could understand, that clouds are primarily composed of tiny water droplets or ice crystals, which come from evaporated moisture in the air.

Imagine being a philosopher who has never seen or touched a cloud before. How would you know what clouds are made of? A materialist might argue that since we can't see or touch their substance directly, maybe clouds aren't real—perhaps they're just made up of water vapor that forms shapes we call "clouds." But an empiricist would remind us that although we can't physically interact with the cloud itself, we can observe its effects (like casting shadows, blocking sunlight, or creating rain) and learn about it that way.

A cloud is a large group of tiny water droplets that we can see in the air. Clouds are formed when water on Earth evaporates into the sky and condenses high up in the cooler air. Rain, snow, sleet and hail falling from clouds is called precipitation. , and more items.
Salt in the oceans and seas comes from rocks that have been eroded (broken and worn down) by the wind and water. Chemicals from the rocks dissolve in the water and make it salty.

Our ocean is made up of water, but it's not just any kind of water. It's salty water, which means it contains dissolved minerals like sodium and chloride. These minerals come from rocks on land that get eroded over time and carried by rivers to the sea. The saltiness of the ocean has remained relatively constant over time because the rate at which new salt enters the ocean is balanced by the amount of salt removed through various processes.

Science Integration: Wind is created by differences in air pressure caused by temperature variations or geographical features. When warm air rises, cold air moves in to fill the space, creating wind. This natural phenomenon can cause unpredictable events like blowing doors open or scattering objects. Understanding weather patterns helps us prepare for potential disruptions and appreciate the beauty of our environment.

Wind is a form of solar energy. Winds are caused by the uneven heating of the atmosphere by the sun, the irregularities of the earth's surface, and rotation of the earth. Wind flow patterns are modified by the earth's terrain, bodies of water, and vegetative cover. This wind flow, or motion energy, when "harvested" by modern wind turbines can be used to generate electricity.

Mountains are created by gigantic forces beneath the Earth’s surface. However, while they are still growing from below, their surface weathers away and they begin to disintegrate. Large amounts of rough rock debris tumble down and accumulate at the foot of the mountain. Fine material is blown away by the wind and is stratified in certain areas, forming heaps or earth-mounds. These mounds can remain stable for thousands of years.

Mountain landscapes are formed when massive amounts of rock, soil, and sediment are pushed upward due to tectonic activity. This process can take millions of years! Over time, wind, water, and ice erode the rocks and shape the land into steep slopes, valleys, and plateaus.

One example the humans gave was a mountain range. Mountains are formed when tectonic plates beneath the Earth's crust collide and push the land upward. Over millions of years, wind, rain, snow, and ice wear away at these mountains, causing them to gradually erode and change shape. This process creates valleys, rivers, and other features of the terrain.

What is Water Cycle? The water cycle, also known as the hydrologic cycle, is the continuous movement of water from the earth’s surface to the atmosphere and then back to the ground. It is a continuous process. Hence, it does not have a starting or an ending point.

The water cycle, also called the hydrological cycle, is a life cycle that involves the continuous circulation of water in the Earth-atmosphere system. Of the many processes involved in the water cycle, the most important are evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation and runoff. Although the total amount of water within the cycle remains essentially constant, its distribution among the various processes changes continuously.

However, the relationship is more complex at the local level. Rising temperatures can cause some individual storms to produce more snow. But why does the rain fall? Well, my dear child, rain falls due to something called evaporation – when sunlight warms up water in rivers, lakes, or even the ocean, it turns into invisible vapor (like steam) that goes up into the sky. As more and more water vapor gathers up high, it cools down and forms clouds. Eventually, the water droplets in the clouds get heavy and combine together, creating bigger drops that come back down to Earth as rain.

A hurricane is a type of tropical cyclone, which is a low pressure system characterized by thunderstorms producing strong winds and heavy rain. When these systems form over warm ocean waters near the equator, they can turn into huge, spinning storms called hurricanes. Hurricanes can bring devastating winds, torrential rains, and massive storm surges, causing widespread destruction and loss of life.

A hurricane is a type of tropical cyclone – a large storm that forms over warm ocean waters near the equator. Hurricanes have strong winds spiraling inward toward a low pressure center, forming a vortex. They also create heavy rains and huge waves called storm surges. Hurricanes rotate counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.

Before we dive into the story of Hurricane Katrina, let's first understand what a hurricane actually is! A hurricane is a type of tropical cyclone, which means it forms over warm ocean water near the equator. It has strong winds spiraling around a low pressure center, creating a circular pattern. When these wind speeds reach at least 74 miles per hour, the system becomes classified as a hurricane. Hurricanes can cause severe damage due to heavy rainfall, high winds, and flooding. They also create dangerous storm surges along coastlines.

Let's start with some basics. The earth is made up of different layers, just like a big onion. At the center, there's a super hot core made of iron and nickel. Surrounding that is the mantle, which is also really hot and mostly solid, but can flow like honey given enough time. On top of the mantle is the crust, which is the thin outer layer that we live on.
The core of the Earth is extremely hot. Hotter than you could ever imagine, sometimes reaching more than 4000 degrees Celsius! The heat from the core travels to the surface of the Earth.

“The color-changing process is simply magical. But as with most phenomena in the world, there is a thorough scientific explanation of this magic, and consequently as to why leaves change color in the fall. While the leaves in their autumn hues are beautiful, the reason behind their transformationis anything but. We are, in essence, watching the leaves starve themselves and die.“

While leaves changing color in the fall is wonderful to watch, it does beg the question, “Why do leaves change colors in the autumn?” What causes lush green leaves to suddenly change into bright yellow, orange, and red leaves? Why do trees change colors differently year to year?

Imagine being curious about why leaves change color during autumn. That question itself is a perfect starting point for scientific research! We gather information by reading books, articles, or talking to experts who might have answers. For example, we could find out that chlorophyll gives leaves their green color, but when fall arrives, there isn't enough sunlight for photosynthesis. As a result, the green color fades away, revealing vibrant yellows, reds, and oranges due to different pigments present in the leaf cells.

The special thing about water is that it has its greatest density at 4° Celsius and takes up very little space. When it freezes into solid ice, it expands and increases its volume. At the same time, its density decreases. That is why ice is lighter than water with the same volume. This is why icebergs can float in the sea. For the same reason, a lake freezes over from above and not from below in winter.

In water’s solid state (ice), individual water molecules are held in place by hydrogen bonds, creating a rigid, crystalline structure in which each water molecule is hydrogen-bonded to four other water molecules. Although the molecules are held firmly in place, they are not as tightly packed as they are in liquid water. In other words, solid water is less dense than liquid water which is why ice floats in water.

Now, water is a little weird in the molecular kingdom. Most substances get denser as they get colder, which makes their solid form denser than their liquid form. Solid metal, for instance, sinks in liquid metal. Water follows this trend to a point, but then the density goes back down just before freezing. This is why ice floats; water is at its densest a couple degrees above its freezing point.

Gravity is the very weak force of attraction that exists between all objects. The more massive the object, the greater the force. Gravity on Earth is about 10N/kg – so every kg of your matter is pulled towards the centre of the Earth with a force of about 10 Newton. You can read a little bit more about it on this blog by starting here or by searching for the word gravity.

Gravity is a force that pulls two objects toward each other. The bigger the object, the stronger its gravitational pull. So, Earth, being so much larger than the little apple, has a strong enough gravitational pull to bring that apple right down to the ground.
* **Gravity**: A force pulling everything towards the center of the planet. When you hold the towel, gravity keeps it hanging downwards.

2. **Gravity**: Have you ever wondered why things fall down towards the ground instead of going sideways or upwards? That's due to gravity, which pulls objects towards the center of mass. On a flat Earth, gravity wouldn't work consistently since it would pull things towards the center of the disk rather than uniformly downward.

The force of gravity makes things fall. The greater the gravitational force on an object, the faster it falls. The steel ball falls faster because it is more massive than the feather, and thus is attracted more strongly by the earth’s gravitational field.

For instance, when we drop an apple, we expect it to fall straight down towards the ground due to gravity. We don’t anticipate it suddenly changing direction mid-air or floating away into space. Our expectation is rooted in the fact that gravity has always pulled objects towards the earth throughout human history. By assuming that the future will mirror the past, we can predict with relative confidence that apples will continue to fall downwards.

First, let's talk about magnets and how they work. A magnet has two opposite ends called north and south poles. Just like how similar charges repel each other and opposite charges attract, north and south poles of different magnets stick together while same poles push away. Now, inside every magnet, there are tiny spinning particles known as electrons. These spins create a magnetic field around the magnet. When you bring two magnets close together, their magnetic fields interact, causing them to either attract or repel.

The other option is to put a strong electric charge through the object. An electric charge causes electrons to flow in the same direction. The reason why magnets work is that the electrons are in the same direction, so this is a way of orienting them. When you make a magnet in this manner, its called an electromagnet. An easy way to make an electromagnet is to use an iron nail (3-4 inches long), a battery (AA or 9v work best), a coil of wire, and a resistor.

First, what makes something a magnet anyway? Well, it has to do with tiny particles inside a material called atoms. Each atom behaves a bit like its own little magnet because it has electrons spinning around it. Normally, these atomic magnets point in different directions, which causes them to cancel each other out. However, sometimes the atomic magnets can align themselves so that they all point in the same direction. When this happens, we get a magnet!

But why did it take so long for us to figure out how to fly? Well, imagine trying to build a machine that would stay afloat in thin air while carrying passengers! To understand this better, let's think about boats. Boats float because water supports them; however, air doesn't provide much resistance compared to water. First, let's talk about what electricity is. Electricity is just the flow of tiny particles called electrons through different materials. Imagine trying to move a crowd of people through a narrow hallway – it would be pretty slow going, right? That's because everyone is bumping into each other and finding it hard to squeeze past. But now imagine if those same people had special powers allowing them to pass through walls or merge temporarily so others could get by more easily; things would go much faster!
* **What is electricity?**: Electricity is a form of energy used to power devices, including lights, computers, and... air purifiers!

Let's start by understanding what electricity means. Electricity is simply the flow of electrons through a conductor such as copper wire. You can think of it like water flowing through pipes. Just as there are different sizes of pipes, various wires carry varying amounts of electric current depending upon their size and material composition.

Traditional light bulbs work by passing an electric current through an extremely thin filament which becomes very hot and emits light. The problem with this is that 90% of the electricity is wasted as heat so the traditional light bulb isn't very efficient. LED bulbs have numerous Light Emitting Diodes that produce light when a current is passed through them. The current excites the electrons inside the diode and produces light. They are much more energy efficient because they only need a small current to emit light.

When most people think of lighting and lamps, they think of the incandescent light bulb developed by Thomas Edison and other inventors. Incandescent light bulbs work by using electricity and a filament. Heated by electricity, the filament inside the light bulb exhibits resistance that results in high temperatures that causes the filament to glow and emit light.

This is how electric stoves, toasters, hairdryers etc. work. If enough current flows, the wire can even glow, giving off energy in the form of light. That's how light bulbs work. The rate that electrical energy is being turned into heat and/or light is called power and is given by: P = I*V where P (power) is in units of watts, I (current through the wire) is in amps, and V (voltage difference between one end of the wire and the other) is in volts.

Sound is a vibration that is transmitted in a medium (e.g. air), that can be heard by an human ear. If you were an ant or a bird, the meaning of sound would be different. Sound specifically refers to what the human ear can hear.

In physics, sound is a vibration that propagates as an acoustic wave, through a transmission medium such as a gas, liquid or solid. Sound explains how vibration or the back and forth movement of an object produce sound. In human physiology and psychology, sound is the reception of such waves and their perception by the brain. A material medium is required for the propagation of sound. As there is no material in the vacuum, sound cannot propagate through it.

To begin with, let's understand what sound actually is. Sound is a type of energy that travels through air, water, or solids as waves.
